quotes.text: No, this isn't more techno/industrial metal ala Circle of Dust, but it is smoking hot – and incredibly infectious – electronica with a really heavy and trance-like vibe. The kicker is this: unlike most electronic stuff you hear on BPM or the radio, these songs have memorable melodies and words tagged to the intense and erotic beats.
I haven't heard a better programmer than Klayton, his beats, ambient effects and keys just mesmerizing.

The original Celldweller self-titled debut was a monumental release in the world of electronica, and it set the stage for the plethora of material that Klayton would subsequently release for entertainment of all forms, to include motion pictures and video games. Not one to be content with the status quo, Klayton has remixed many of the songs from this release previously on the double CD The Beta Cessions.

About the only deficiency here – it would have been nice to have some liner notes or a little history about the origin of these tunes and about the formation/history of Celldweller, one of the most innovative and creative acts of the digital era.
In truly Klayton style, the self-titled debut was reissued in 2024 in digital download (Bandcamp) and earlier this year with more grandeur than ever on CD and vinyl versions (FiXT).
the production as a whole stands out, having a clean modern metal vibe backed by punchy drums that are upfront and clear - as you would expect from what is essentially a dance album.
Zardonic clearly does not try to anticipate or second-guess what a dance audience thinks.
Bret Autry, AKA 'Blue Stahli' is definitely a musician from the 'more is more' school of sonic bombardment.
Once acclimatised to the full-speed ahead approach, the listener may be able to appreciate the cheeky humour of the composer, his skill with instruments, and the myriad sonic flourishes
Because of this, there's a refreshing economy in his compositions, and, like his day-job suggests, there is no room for filler – only killer.

Klayton himself resembles a cyber-culture analogue of Bowie's Ziggy Stardust, and that this conclusion to his 'Blackstar' song cycle is released within weeks of Bowie's final opus, also entitled 'Blackstar'.

Over the course of two decades mastermind Klayton has pioneered the sound of future rock with his music project Celldweller. Known for exploring different genres and shattering the boundaries of definitions, he's continued to expand his horizons even further since starting out with Circle of Dust, including his other ventures Scandroid and FreqGen.

Fifth instalment Satellites feels like a much darker album in comparison to other Celldweller releases, and this is no coincidence. Being recorded under the backdrop of a global pandemic, Klayton translates the frustrations and isolation felt over the past couple of years into a soundscape that is a release of aggressive fury.

This is without a doubt the heaviest Celldweller material he has crafted yet, presented in his usual genre-defying mashup of music influences. It traverses synthwave, drum and bass, electro rock, industrial metal and everything between.
Just as listeners think they've got the record pinned down, it throws another exciting curveball out of nowhere that completely subverts expectations.

This is probably the most metal that a Celldweller track has ever been. Thankfully this is achieved without veering too far into the more organic instrumentation and is balanced with healthy doses of electro.
There are very few artists who are able to blend such differing genres so majestically and he continues to evolve his sound in new, exciting ways.
This is probably the most traditional Celldweller song on Satellites and at times has a real old-school feel to it.

It switches between these different influences in the blink of an eye but does so without missing a beat. It feels like Klayton brings his full range in this single number both vocally and in terms of instrumentation.
